intro.html: Some words describe people and creatures spoiling for a fight; others name the side we fight against and the ways fights end. Many come from Latin words for battle: bellum (war) in bellicose and belligerent, pugnus (fist) in pugnacious, and miles (soldier) in militant.

Ready to fight: hostile, belligerent, bellicose, pugnacious, truculent, militant. The other side: adversary. Ending the fight: truce (a pause), armistice (an end to the fighting) and diplomacy (talking it out).

words.def: unfriendly; showing that you want to fight or oppose
words.ex: The cat gave the new puppy a {hostile} stare and a low hiss.
words.ctx: The visiting team expected a {hostile} crowd, but the home fans surprised them with polite applause and even a few friendly cheers.
words.etym: From Latin hostilis, from hostis, “an enemy, a stranger.”

mn.cue: HOST-ILE: a HOST who wants a fight
mn.text: Felix answers his door with a scowl and crossed arms: “No visitors!” He is the most {hostile} host on the street.

scene.alt: A scowling man at his door shouts at two children who have come with a gift.

words.def: acting angry and ready to fight
words.ex: The {belligerent} customer shouted at the cashier over a ten-cent coupon.
words.ctx: Instead of apologizing for the fender bender, the driver grew {belligerent}: he jumped out of his car, waved his arms and dared the other driver to do something about it.
words.etym: From Latin belligerare, “to wage war”: bellum (war) + gerere (to carry on).

mn.cue: BELL-igerent: the goat with the BELL charges
mn.text: The goat with the bell around his neck lowers his horns and charges at anyone who comes near the barn. He is {belligerent}.

scene.alt: An angry goat wearing a bell charges at a farmer, who runs away.

words.def: eager to fight or go to war; warlike by nature
words.ex: The {bellicose} rooster picked a fight with every bird in the yard.
words.ctx: The old general’s speeches grew more {bellicose} each year; he talked of nothing but battles, enemies and the glory of war.

mn.text: Every single morning, the rooster puffs up his chest and dares every animal in the yard to fight him. Fighting is his nature: he is {bellicose}.

scene.alt: A puffed-up rooster challenges a worried duck and a bored pig to a fight.

words.ex: The {pugnacious} little terrier barked at dogs five times his size.
words.ctx: Unlike his calm older sister, Dev was {pugnacious}; he would argue with anyone about anything, from baseball scores to the color of the sky.
words.etym: From Latin pugnax, “fond of fighting,” from pugnare, “to fight,” from pugnus, “fist.”

mn.cue: PUG-NACIOUS: a PUG ready to fight
mn.text: The tiny pug plants his feet and growls at an elephant a hundred times his size: “Come on!” He is {pugnacious}.

scene.alt: A tiny pug growls at a huge, startled elephant.

words.def: quick to argue or fight; fierce and defiant
words.ex: The {truculent} toddler crossed his arms and refused to put on his shoes.
words.ctx: Asked to explain why he was late, the {truculent} teenager only scowled, folded his arms and muttered that it was none of their business.
words.etym: From Latin truculentus, “fierce, savage,” from trux, “wild, fierce.”

mn.text: Theo sits in his toy truck with his arms crossed and a fierce scowl: “Mine! Go away!” He is {truculent}.

scene.alt: A scowling toddler sits in his toy wagon, arms crossed, refusing to share with a girl.

words.def: an opponent; someone you compete or fight against
words.ex: In the chess final, Maya faced her toughest {adversary}: her own grandfather.
words.ctx: The two lawyers were good friends outside the courtroom, but inside it they were {adversaries}, each working hard to win the case.
words.etym: From Latin adversarius, “opponent,” from adversus, “turned against”: ad (toward) + vertere (to turn).

mn.text: In the tug-of-war, it is Jonah versus Rosa, each pulling the other way: they are {adversaries}.

scene.alt: Two teens pull hard on opposite ends of a rope in a tug-of-war.

words.def: fighting hard and aggressively for a cause
words.ex: The {militant} members of the garden club demanded that every lawn in town become a vegetable patch.
words.ctx: Most neighbors wanted to write polite letters about the park, but a {militant} few wanted to block the road and refuse to leave until the bulldozers were gone.
words.etym: From Latin militare, “to serve as a soldier,” from miles, “soldier,” the root of military.

mn.cue: MILIT-ANT: an ANT army for a cause
mn.text: The ants march in a fierce line with tiny signs: SAVE OUR HILL! They will fight hard for their anthill: they are {militant}.

scene.alt: A line of determined ants marches with little signs that say Save Our Hill.

words.def: an agreement to stop fighting for a while
words.ex: The two brothers called a {truce} in their pillow fight so they could eat breakfast.
words.ctx: The cats had battled over the sunny windowsill all week, but a {truce} held at dinnertime: side by side, they ate from their bowls without a single hiss.
words.etym: From Middle English trewes, the plural of trewe, “a pledge,” a word related to true.

mn.cue: TRUCE: a TRUE pause, for now
mn.text: In the middle of their snowball fight, Kai waves a white flag: “Truce! Cocoa break!” For now, the fight is paused: it is a {truce}.

labels.text: TRUCE: a pause in the fight

scene.alt: In a snowy yard, one boy waves a white flag and another offers him hot cocoa, pausing their snowball fight.

words.def: an agreement between two sides at war to stop fighting
words.ex: The {armistice} was signed at dawn, and by noon the fighting had stopped all along the border.
words.ctx: After four long years of war, the {armistice} finally brought the fighting to an end, though the two nations still needed months to work out a full peace treaty.
words.etym: From Modern Latin armistitium: arma (weapons) + -stitium (a standing still), formed like solstice.
words.note: A truce may be only a short pause; an armistice ends the fighting of a war, usually while a full peace treaty is worked out.

mn.text: The two kings shake hands over a signed scroll, and both armies put down their arms and stand still. The {armistice} ends the war.

scene.alt: Two kings reach toward each other over a peace scroll, each beside his own flag.

words.def: the work of managing relations between nations; also, skill in handling people tactfully
words.ex: With a little {diplomacy}, Lila got both brothers to share the last slice of cake.
words.ctx: The border quarrel could have led to war, but patient {diplomacy} won out; after months of quiet talks, the two countries signed a treaty.
words.etym: From French diplomatie, from diploma, an official paper, from Greek diploma, “a paper folded in two.”

mn.cue: DIPLOMA-cy: talk it out, then sign the paper
mn.text: Pip and Sami are fighting over the tree swing, so Lila sits them down, listens to each and gets them to sign a turn-taking deal. That is {diplomacy}.

scene.alt: A girl holds out a written deal for two boys, who agree to take turns on the swing.

after.cap: From picking a fight to making peace.

after.html: Bellicose and belligerent share Latin bellum, war. Bellicose usually describes a person’s nature (a bellicose ruler who loves war); belligerent describes how someone is acting (a belligerent customer shouting right now). A truce is a pause, while an armistice ends the fighting of a war.

opts.s: Even after losing the argument, Rex stayed {truculent}, scowling and refusing to shake hands.
opts.why: Scowling and refusing to shake hands is fierce and defiant: truculent.

items.q: After four years, the two nations signed an ______ that ended the fighting of the war for good. Which word fits?
items.why: An armistice is an agreement between sides at war to stop fighting. A truce may be only a short pause.

items.q: True or false: bellicose and belligerent both come from Latin bellum, war.
items.why: True. Bellicose means warlike by nature; belligerent means acting ready to fight.

items.q: Which word is the opposite of adversary?
items.why: An adversary is on the other side; an ally is on your side. Opponent, rival and foe are synonyms.

items.q: The Latin word pugnus, hidden in pugnacious, means…
items.why: Pugnus means fist, and pugnare means to fight: a pugnacious person is quick to put up his fists or to argue. (The pug dog is just a handy sound-alike.)

items.q: Type the word for skill in handling nations and people tactfully, which comes from a Greek word for a paper folded in two.
items.why: Diplomacy comes through French from diploma, an official paper, from Greek for a paper folded in two.
